scenes.narration: This is Strasbourg, today in France. In July, a woman named Frau Troffea stepped into the street and began to dance.

icons.ai: a cute cartoon medieval woman in a long dress dancing wildly with arms in the air
icons.name: woman dancing

scenes.narration: She danced for days. No music, no reason, and she couldn't stop.
Within weeks, dozens of people had joined her. Some accounts say it grew to hundreds.

icons.ai: a cute cartoon medieval woman in a long dress dancing wildly with arms in the air
icons.name: woman dancing

scenes.narration: Here's the strange part. The city's doctors said the cure was to dance it out.

photos.q: Dancing pilgrims at Molenbeek Hondius Brueghel
photos.caption: DANCING MANIA

scenes.narration: So, according to the old chronicles, the council hired musicians, and even set up a stage.

icons.ai: a cute cartoon medieval musician playing a drum and a flute
icons.name: drum

scenes.narration: It only made things worse. Some say dancers collapsed from exhaustion, but historians still argue about deaths.
So what was going on? Strasbourg had just been hit by famine, disease and freezing winters.
Many historians think it was mass psychogenic illness: fear and stress spreading through a crowd, almost like a virus.
Others blamed ergot, a mold on rye bread that can cause spasms and hallucinations.
In the end, the dancers were taken to a shrine of Saint Vitus in the hills. And slowly, the dancing stopped.
If the whole town started dancing, would you join in? Yes or no?
